analysis: Per trial: QA accuracy pre vs post feedback injection (paired difference), and a 'feedback incorporated' boolean checked by querying semantic memory for the corrected fact and by whether subsequent answers change. Paired t-test on accuracy delta. Report the fraction of trials where the correction is retrievable from semantic memory (mechanism check).
failure_condition: Fail if post-feedback accuracy is not higher than pre-feedback accuracy (paired t-test, alpha=0.05) across trials, OR if the injected correction cannot be retrieved from semantic memory afterward (the feedback went nowhere), OR if accuracy IMPROVES but the corrected fact is absent from memory (improvement without mechanism — likely prompt leakage, not adaptation).
hypothesis: After corrective feedback is injected into semantic memory (a corrected answer to a question the system got wrong), the system's accuracy on a re-run will improve, because semantic recall feeds corrected facts back into the workspace prompt context.
limitations: This is supervised correction, not autonomous learning: the feedback is handed to the system, not discovered. It measures the retrieval-and-use path, not the ability to detect one's own errors. The before/after design risks prompt-order effects (the correction may simply linger in context). Only tests correction of factual answers, not strategy adaptation — strategy selection is Learning's job and needs its own protocol.
name: adaptation_after_feedback
research_question: Can the system incorporate explicit corrective feedback into its semantic memory and then use it — i.e., does it get a second attempt right because the correction was stored and retrieved, not because it was repeated in the prompt?
